title: GPU runtime profiling deep dive with Aperture Tech
summary: Deep technical session focused on GPU runtime profiling: kernel selection heuristics, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA graphs/cuda-graph warmup, KV-cache and batching strategies, quantization impacts, and VPC/on-prem constraints for an upcoming pilot.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we have about 55 minutes, i'll hand off to Jordan to cover the profiling we ran, and then we'll dig into your questions about on-prem and VPC.
[00:14] Jordan (Redwood SE): cool, thanks Alex. quick context — Aperture mentioned they're seeing 80-120 ms tail latency on p4d instances for 4k-contexts, and want to reduce cost without regressing quality. i'm going to walk through kernel selection, tensorRT-llm comparsions, and how cuda graphs affect warmup.
[00:30] Priya (Aperture): hey, yes that's right. our main concern is tail latency at 99.9 and also KV cache hot path, we use long-lived sessions for chat history and we see big spikes when cache misses happen.
[00:45] Jordan: okay, great. first, kernel selection: our runtime profiles model layer by layer, chooses kernels based on model architecture, sequence length distribution, and hardware. so for attn variants we choose fused attention kernels when sequence small, but fallback to standard matmul when sequence grows — that decision reduces memory pressure and improves throughput. sometimes the heuristic picks a less-optimal kernel for very skewed seq-len distributions — that's why per-workload profiling matters.
[01:10] Miguel (Aperture): are these heuristics deterministic? we need reproducible perf for SLA tests.
[01:18] Jordan: good q. they're deterministic given the same runtime config and inputs, but we allow a "kernel selection override" in configs so you can pin kernel choices for benchmarking. i recommend pinning when you run your SLA validation runs.
[01:30] Alex: (interject) also we log the chosen kernel per-request in the trace so you can audit which path was used.
[01:38] Priya: nice, that helps. what about tensorRT-llm vs vLLM — we've heard both recommended.
[01:45] Jordan: short answer: TensorRT-LLM often gives the best single-request latency for FP16 / int8 quantized models on NVIDIA hardware when you can pay the compilation and memory cost. vLLM is great for CPU and multi-tenant GPU scenarios where dynamic batching and memory footprint matter; also vllm has very good KV cache sharing logic but lacks some of TensorRT's fused kernel optimizations. long answer — depends on model size, batch patterns, and how much precompile time you can accept.
[02:12] Lena (Aperture): our workload is mostly interactive chat with many small requests and occasional long-context retriever calls. sounds like we care about small batch latency and cache efficiency.
[02:22] Jordan: exactly — for that pattern we typically prefer a runtime that does continuous batching with aggressive prefix/KV caching. Redwood runtime supports both: we can run TensorRT-LLM compiled variants for hot models and fall back to a vLLM-like path for cold or dynamic cases. the hybrid approach often gives best unit economics.
[02:40] Tom (Aperture): how does CUDA graphs come into play? we saw notes about cudagraphs reducing CPU overhead.
[02:47] Jordan: good point. CUDA graphs let you capture a sequence of GPU ops and replay with much lower CPU overhead and kernel launch latency. for stable prompt shapes and compiled kernels, we can capture execution into a CUDA graph after a short warmup. that usually improves p50/p95 by eliminating CPU serialization. caveats — graphs are less flexible with dynamic shapes and you need a warmup step; also graph capture interacts with memory allocators and certain non-deterministic kernels.
[03:12] Priya: you mentioned warmup — how long? for our sessions we rotate models often.
[03:18] Jordan: typical warmup is 5-20 iterations depending on graph complexity; for many of our tests we capture after ~10 representative requests. for very dynamic environments we capture multiple graphs per shape and select at runtime.
[03:28] Alex: we also support a lightweight graph-less fallback that still uses optimized kernels but has slightly higher p95.
[03:34] Miguel: on the NV infra we run, we use a mix of g5 and a10g for cost reasons. do you recommend p4d or triton-optimized instances?
[03:43] Jordan: gpus matter. TensorRT's wins are more pronounced on A100s and H100s but you can still see improvements on G5 family. the key is picking instance types that give enough GPU memory for compiled engines and batch sizes you need. for cost-conscious deployments, our recommendation is to run throughput benchmarks across both families and choose the sweet spot. we can share a benchmarking script.
[04:03] Priya: please do. also, how does kv cache eviction/breakdown look in your telemetry? we sometimes see full re-encode on cache misses.
[04:12] Samira (SE): on KV cache, we do prefix caching and allow atomic prefix slices to be cached; cache hit paths are highly optimized to avoid re-encoding. cache misses incur the typical re-encode + attention recompute cost. we also offer a config for partial-cache recomposition to avoid full re-encode when only suffix changed.
[04:34] Priya: hmm that's interesting — partial recomposition might help.
[04:38] Jordan: yes, tradeoff is complexity vs memory. quantization also impacts cache: int8 FP8-style quantization can reduce memory and speed up GEMMs but you need to be careful about KV cache quantized storage and dequantize overhead for attention.
[04:56] Miguel: are you seeing accuracy regressions with int8 in your tests?
[04:59] Jordan: small regressions on some models; we provide quantization profiles per-model and recommend per-prompt regression tests. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles and run regression checks against a holdout eval set.
[05:12] Lena: what's the operational story for VPC/on-prem? we have compliance teams concerned about data egress and KMS.
[05:20] Alex: Redwood Private supports customer-managed networking and KMS/HSM integration, audit logs, and SOC2 artifacts. for on-prem we ship a control-plane-lite package and an inference plane that runs in your cluster. networking can be fully air-gapped if required, but we need an initial onboarding handshake. we also support SAML SSO and RBAC.
[05:38] Tom: any gotchas with CUDA graphs and on-prem clusters? our infra team worries about driver mismatches.
[05:44] Jordan: yes driver/kernel/userland mismatches are the biggest pain point. CUDA graphs and TensorRT compiled engines are sensitive to driver and cuDNN versions. we recommend a controlled image (we provide recommended AMIs/containers) and an initial compatibility test. part of our onboarding includes a driver/stack checklist.
[06:02] Priya: can you run a quick walkthrough of an example profile you collected? numbers help.
[06:07] Jordan: sure, i'll read from a recent run. model: 7B open-arch variant, fp16, compiled with TensorRT-LLM. workload: 1 request/sec, burst to 8 rps, avg prompt len 128 tokens, decode length 64.
[06:24] Jordan: observed metrics: p50 generation latency ~45ms, p95 ~110ms, p99 ~220ms. CUDA graph capture reduced p95 from 160ms to 110ms. continuous batching with prefetched KV cache improved throughput by ~30% for batched inference vs unbatched. kernel selection log showed fused-attn kernel for first 20 layers then fallback on later layers due to memory footprint causing a change in kernel selection at step ~30.
[06:53] Priya: that p99 is still higher than we'd like. what contributed to the 220ms outlier?
[06:58] Jordan: main contributors were cache miss + graph capture happening concurrently leading to a synchronous allocation, and one fallback to a non-fused kernel due to a transient memory spike. we have mitigations: reserve additional workspace memory to avoid fallback, pre-warm graphs, and pin kernels.
[07:14] Alex: also we saw one kernel launch serialized by a CPU-side lock in the particular runtime shim we used in that test; that was fixed in our internal branch and backported to the runtime we run in hosted.
[07:25] Miguel: do you have a reproducible benchmark script we can run in our environment? ideally with p99 profiling and kernel logs
[07:31] Jordan: yes, we'll send a bench repo and a runbook. it collects kernel-choice traces, CUDA graph captures, and per-token latency histograms. it outputs a csv and a small dashboard.
[07:44] Priya: roadmap question — if we go hybrid (tensorrt for hot path, vllm for cold), how do you orchestrate fallbacks? do you support automated route-based fallbacks?
[07:54] Samira: we support smart routing policies — you can route by latency, cost, or region. for example route hot sessions to dedicated TensorRT pool, and route underutilized or dynamic shapes to a vLLM pool. fallback can be automatic on congestion. it's pluggable in the config.
[08:09] Tom: licensing for TensorRT engines — any restrictions we should know of?
[08:13] Alex: TensorRT is NVIDIA stack, you need compatible drivers; our offering uses TensorRT-LLM binaries that we manage in hosted; for private you can either use our validated images or supply your own. we can share a doc describing compat and licensing considerations.
[08:25] Lena: curious about cost modeling: how much cheaper is hybrid typically?
[08:29] Jordan: depends, but hybrid can reduce cost per token by 20-45% depending on your shape distribution because you avoid paying compiled-engine memory overhead for cold models and use vLLM-like runtime efficiency when tracing is not worth it.
[08:43] Priya: ok, can we capture specific next steps here?
[08:47] Alex: yes — recap and next steps:
[08:50] Alex: 1) Redwood to share benchmarking repo + runbook (includes kernel logs, cuda graph toggles, and recommended AMI/container). 2) Aperture to run bench on representative p4d/g5 instances and share results. 3) Redwood to provide quantization profiles for 7B model variant and suggested eval prompts. 4) schedule a 1:1 pilot setup meeting for lab access and driver validation. 5) Redwood to share Private deployment compatibility checklist and SOC2/KMS docs.
[09:12] Priya: sounds good. target to have bench results in two weeks? we can try to turn around in 10 business days.
[09:20] Alex: great, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the repo link.
[09:24] (end)\n\nNotes on transcription: occasional speaker mis-attribution by auto-transcription; some proper nouns like "vLLM" transcribed as "v-LLM" or "vllm" in interim artifacts. references: bench repo link (sent post-call), perf spreadsheet (to be shared), Redwood Private docs link.
